advances: Ordinary continuous maximal depth in the critical inverse-power class.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Let $P(u,y)=\int_{u\cdot(x-y)\ge0} f(x)\,dx$ for unit normals $u$. The raw depth at $y$ is the minimum of $P(u,y)$ because tightening a containing halfspace through $y$ can only decrease its mass. Joint continuity by dominated convergence and compactness of the sphere give continuity of the minimum. The depth is positive at an interior point by a positive density lower bound on a small ball, and zero on and outside the boundary by a supporting or separating hyperplane. At $y\ne0$ the cap with normal $y/\|y\|$ has mass at most $\int_{\|x\|\ge\|y\|} f(x)\,dx$. Thus the maximum is attained at an interior point $y$.

At such a point the compact active set of minimizing normals has zero in its convex hull. Otherwise strict separation gives $u\cdot v>\delta>0$ on that set, and $u\cdot v>\delta/2$ in a neighborhood of it. A displacement to $y-\varepsilon v$ adds for every near-active normal a slab of width at least $\varepsilon\delta/2$ through a fixed small ball about $y$ on which $f$ has a positive lower bound. Its mass is uniformly bounded below by a positive multiple of $\varepsilon$, since all sections in the central half of that ball have a common area lower bound. On the remaining compact set the cap masses have a positive gap above the minimum that persists under small displacements. This contradicts maximality. A finite convex combination of active normals therefore equals zero with strictly positive coefficients, and their through-$y$ halfspaces cover all of $\mathbb R^r$.

Apply the radial construction in the proof of critical-inverse-power-simplex-projective-rigidity about $y$. The radial body is compact, full-dimensional and preserves the full mass and each through-$y$ cap mass. The origin has normalized depth $D(f)$ in the radial body. The active caps translate to a covering family of equal normalized mass $D(f)$ on the body, so its maximal depth is exactly $D(f)$. The uniform-body theorem 03bc771bddd39a8a gives $D(f)\ge\gamma_r$ and makes the radial body a simplex in the equality case. In that case its origin must be the centroid, since any other simplex point has a barycentric coordinate greater than $1/(r+1)$, whose vertex cap cuts a fraction strictly less than $\gamma_r$. The preceding classification now gives the positive-chart representation.

Conversely, for a centroid-centered simplex gauge profile, all through-center cap fractions agree with those of the reference simplex by polar integration, and the center has depth $\gamma_r$ by 03bc771bddd39a8a. The canonical vertex caps at barycentric threshold $1/(r+1)$ each have fraction $\gamma_r$ and cover all of space since the barycentric coordinates sum to one. They bound every candidate's depth by $\gamma_r$. On the positive chart the pullback of $a\cdot x\ge b$ is $(a+b\ell)\cdot v\ge b$ in the profile variable $v$, and the inverse pullback follows from the inverse chart with opposite sign. Thus all proper halfspace traces match in both directions; a degenerate containing trace is the whole domain and adds only the trivial mass-one choice. The pushforward preserves the mass of every trace. Points outside the open support have depth zero, as above. This proves sufficiency and identifies the chart center as a deepest point.
statement: Let $r\ge2$ and let $f$ be a nonnegative Lebesgue density of finite positive mass on $\mathbb R^r$, with full-dimensional positive support and convex extended inverse $(r+1)$st root. Let $D(f)$ denote the supremal normalized closed-halfspace depth over all points, for the probability density $f/\int f$. Then $D(f)\ge\gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r$ and the maximum is attained in the positive interior. Equality holds exactly when, after translating some interior point to $0$, $f(x)\,dx$ is the positive-chart projective pushforward of a normalized gauge profile on a centroid-centered simplex, with the profile and chart conditions of that theorem. The chart center is a deepest point.
title: Sharp ordinary depth equality at the critical inverse power
